notes.meaning: The Lord announces a special day that belongs to Him, when enemy armies will conquer Jerusalem and divide its stolen goods right inside the city walls. The invaders feel so secure in their victory that they sort out their plunder out in the open. God uses this deep trial to begin the final rescue and vindication of His people.

differ.view: Wesley and Benson view this opening prophecy as referring to the Roman destruction of Jerusalem in ancient times.
Gill interprets this not as the ancient Roman conquest, but as a future day when the Lord gathers the nations before converting the Jewish people.

notes.meaning: God permits hostile nations to gather against Jerusalem, plundering homes and treating the residents with cruel violence. Half the inhabitants are led away as captives, but a faithful remnant remains in the city. Even when foreign invaders attack, God stays in complete control of the final outcome for His people.

Just when the city seems completely lost, the Lord steps forward as a warrior to fight against those attacking nations. He defends His people with the same mighty power He showed in ancient battles, such as the deliverance of Israel at the Red Sea. God never leaves His people without hope when their enemies press hardest.

The Lord descends to stand upon the Mount of Olives just east of Jerusalem, displaying His supreme power over the earth. An earthquake splits the mountain into two halves, one moving north and the other south, opening a wide valley running east and west. This split creates an immediate escape route for the besieged people in the city.

differ.view: Jesus will physically return to earth and touch down on the Mount of Olives to inaugurate a thousand-year reign.
God's feet touching the mountain and cleaving it are vivid picture-language for His divine intervention rather than a physical split of the landscape.

notes.meaning: The trapped people flee through this newly opened mountain valley all the way to a place named Azal. Their sudden flight is compared to the terrifying earthquake that struck Judah during the reign of King Uzziah. Then the Lord arrives with all His holy angels and heavenly armies to rescue them completely.

The usual lights of the sky will be darkened during this extraordinary time of judgment and wonder. The natural cycle of sunny warmth and cold frost will fade away before God's majesty. In this strange twilight, ordinary human experience is suspended while God acts.

This unique day belongs to the Lord alone, and its timing is known only to Him. It will be neither normal daylight nor pitch-black night, but a time of mysterious dimness. Yet right when evening approaches, miraculous light will suddenly burst forth to bring comfort and joy.

Fresh, life-giving water will stream out from Jerusalem in two directions, flowing east toward the Dead Sea and west toward the Mediterranean Sea. Unlike seasonal desert streams, these waters will never dry up in summer or freeze in winter. They represent God's continuous, life-giving presence and spiritual blessings spreading outward to heal the world.

differ.view: A physical river will flow both east and west across the reshaped land from Jerusalem.
The living waters symbolize the life-giving gospel and the Holy Spirit flowing continuously from the church into all the world.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early Christian writers and traditional Catholic commentators understand the living waters as the gospel spreading across the earth, and connect them with the water flowing from Christ's pierced side.

notes.meaning: The Lord will be recognized as the one true King over the whole earth, putting an end to all false idols and gods. Everyone will acknowledge Him alone and worship Him under one name. True peace comes when the entire world honors God's rightful authority.

The rugged hills surrounding Jerusalem, from Geba in the north to Rimmon in the south, will be leveled into a wide plain. Jerusalem itself will remain exalted on high, rebuilt fully between its familiar gates and towers. The city will stand prominent and accessible, showing its royal and spiritual dignity before all people.

People will live safely in Jerusalem without fear of war, danger, or exile. The divine curse and threat of utter ruin will be removed forever. Believers can rest in the promise that God keeps His city and people entirely secure.

God will strike the hostile armies that fought against Jerusalem with a sudden and horrific plague. Their bodies will waste away while they are still standing, their eyes will rot in their sockets, and their tongues will rot in their mouths. This terrible judgment shows the sudden ruin that comes upon those who set themselves against God.

The Lord will send sudden panic and wild confusion through the enemy ranks. In their frantic terror, soldiers will grab hold of their companions and turn their weapons against one another. God often defeats the proud by causing them to destroy themselves.

The people of Judah will take part in the fight at Jerusalem against the retreating enemies. In a complete turnaround from earlier looting, God's people will collect immense heaps of gold, silver, and clothing left behind by the surrounding nations. God reverses the losses of His people and crowns their struggle with rich abundance.

The very same wasting plague will fall upon the horses, mules, camels, donkeys, and all other livestock in the enemy camps. The military strength of the invaders will be completely wiped out so none of their war gear remains useful. God's victory leaves no weapon intact that was raised against His people.

The survivors from all the nations that once attacked Jerusalem will turn to the Lord and make an annual pilgrimage to worship Him as King. They will join in celebrating the Feast of Tabernacles, thanking God for His harvest and protective shelter. Former enemies will share in joyful praise alongside the people of God.

differ.view: Surviving nations will physically travel to Jerusalem each year to celebrate the festival during Christ's thousand-year earthly reign.
The Feast of Tabernacles is picture-language for regular, thankful worship offered to Christ in the church age.

notes.meaning: Any family or nation on earth that refuses to go up to Jerusalem to worship the King will face severe drought. Rain will be withheld from their fields, bringing dry seasons and food shortages. Those who ignore God's worship cut themselves off from His life-giving blessings.

Egypt is singled out because it depended on the rising Nile River rather than seasonal rainfall for its crops. Even if Egypt thinks it does not need rain, God warns that the same plague of drought and famine will strike them if they refuse to come. No nation can make itself independent of God's authority.

This penalty will fall upon Egypt and every other nation that fails to keep the Feast of Tabernacles. God enforces a single standard of justice and worship across the entire world. Disobeying the Lord's call always brings loss and punishment.

Holiness will become so widespread that even the small bells on horses' bridles will be engraved with the words 'HOLY TO THE LORD.' In ancient Israel, that sacred motto belonged only on the golden crown of the high priest. At the same time, simple cooking pots in the temple kitchen will be treated as sacred as the sprinkling bowls before the altar.

Every ordinary pot throughout Jerusalem and Judah will be consecrated as holy to the Lord of Hosts, so worshippers can use any vessel to prepare sacrificial meals. The boundary between sacred temple gear and everyday household items will disappear because all of life is dedicated to God. Furthermore, no greedy merchant or ungodly person will ever again defile the house of the Lord.

differ.view: Animal sacrifices will continue in a rebuilt temple as memorials of Christ during the millennium.
Old Testament terms like pots and sacrifices are figures representing the spiritual worship, prayers, and dedicated lives of Christians.
